questions.q: What is the classical baseline used in this lesson, and why is it chosen deliberately simple rather than a tuned model?
options: A single threshold rule on petal length (>= 2.5cm predicts Versicolor), chosen because if the quantum model can't beat even this trivial rule, that's a meaningful, honest result rather than an unfairly rigged comparison
A deep neural network with 50 layers, chosen to make the comparison as difficult as possible for the quantum model
An SVM extensively tuned with grid search over hundreds of hyperparameters
There is no classical baseline used in this lesson at all
questions.explain: A trivial, hand-writable threshold rule is deliberately chosen as the baseline -- if a quantum model can't beat even this, it's a fair and honest signal, not an artificially harsh comparison, consistent with Lesson 4's fair-comparison standard.

questions.q: On the 6-sample held-out evaluation set, what were the measured accuracies of the classical baseline and the quantum classifier?
options: Classical: 100% (6/6); Quantum: 50% (3/6)
Classical: 50%; Quantum: 100%
Both achieved 100% accuracy
Both achieved 50% accuracy
questions.explain: The threshold rule correctly classified all 6 held-out samples, while the single-step-trained quantum classifier correctly classified only the 3 Setosa samples, missing all 3 Versicolor samples, for 50% accuracy.

questions.q: Why did the quantum classifier predict class 0 for every single held-out sample, including all three Versicolor samples?
options: Lesson 24's single gradient step was computed using only the Setosa sample, so it only ever got pushed toward correctly classifying Setosa -- it never received any training signal to separate Versicolor, and ended up biased toward predicting 0 for everything
Because the quantum circuit is fundamentally incapable of ever predicting class 1
Because Versicolor petal measurements are identical to Setosa's in the real dataset
Because the classical baseline interfered with the quantum circuit's predictions
questions.explain: The gradient update only used the Setosa sample's loss, so the model was never pushed to correctly separate Versicolor -- a direct, traceable consequence of single-sample training, not an inherent limitation of quantum circuits.

questions.q: What does this lesson explicitly say the 50% vs 100% benchmark result does NOT establish?
options: That a fully-trained QML model would underperform a classical model on this or any task, or that QML models generally underperform -- a single small experiment doesn't license either generalization
That the classical threshold rule works on this specific held-out set
That the quantum classifier mispredicted all three Versicolor samples
That Setosa and Versicolor are close to linearly separable by petal length
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that this result reflects one specific undertrained model on one specific small evaluation, and does not license any broader claim about QML models generally -- consistent with the course's overall honest, non-overclaiming framing.

questions.q: What would need to change in Lesson 24's training procedure to plausibly prevent this exact failure mode (predicting one class for everything) in a real training run?
options: Update both theta1 and theta2 using gradients averaged or iterated across ALL training samples (not just one), over many iterations, rather than a single step from a single sample
Switch from angle encoding to basis encoding, which would automatically fix the issue
Increase the number of qubits to at least 20, regardless of the dataset's feature count
Nothing can be done; this failure mode is an inherent, unfixable property of quantum classifiers
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly points to training on the full dataset (not just one sample) across many iterations, updating all parameters together, as the fix flagged at the end of Lesson 24 and revisited here.
